title: Running DeepSeek-V4-Flash and Kimi-K3 on Consumer Hardware with SSD Expert Pack (WiCi AI + SGLang Team, LMSYS blog, 2026-08-29)
id_read: blog HTML https://lmsys.org/blog/2026-08-29-sglang-ssd-expert-pack/ ; companion arXiv 2609.18110v1 (SSD-LLaMA) read in part
setup: Intel Ultra5 230F, 32 GB RAM, 2 TB NVMe (bandwidth not stated), RTX 5090 32GB; DeepSeek-V4-Flash MXFP4 GGUF 155.10 GB (pack 147.18), Kimi-K3 Q2_K 38 shards 1009.51 GB (pack 985.61), Kimi 92 routed layers top-16; params/expert counts/DeepSeek top-k not on page; batch 1, 10 requests x 200 tokens; baselines Ollama 0.33.1 (DeepSeek, offload settings not given) and llama.cpp -ngl -1 --cpu-moe -t 16 (Kimi); SGLang GPU expert cache 21 GiB (DeepSeek) / 5 GiB (Kimi), direct I/O, pinned staging

numbers.ratio: implied DeepSeek SSD rate 3.3-3.8 GB/s (my arithmetic)

numbers.what: SSD-LLaMA ablation: all-pack vs GGUF mmap

catalog_numbers_correct.claim: offline repack to per-expert contiguous blocks, direct I/O to aligned pinned buffers; GGUF tensor-oriented

catalog_numbers_correct.true_value: --cpu-moe only on the Kimi llama.cpp baseline; Ollama has no such flag

why: Layout argument transfers (one aligned contiguous extent per expert; our B.md found no slice 4KiB aligned, gate/up 114 MB apart). Speedup does not: GPU with 21 GiB expert cache (hit up to 54%), pinned H2D, baselines at 0.29 tok/s on models 4.7x-31x RAM, no layout-vs-cache ablation in the blog.
quality_loss: none by design (no pruning, top-k unchanged); evidence thin: semantically equivalent answers vs Ollama; Kimi matched 200-token reference
ablation: none in blog; SSD-LLaMA paper has pack ablation 2.6x/4.1x and VRAM cache ablation 2.78x over no cache
limitations: extra SSD space ~ model size, 5-45 min prep, O_DIRECT alignment fail-closed, cache/workload dependent, GPU-only, miss on critical path, no SSD KV offload
contradicts_our_findings: Not a contradiction but suggests our mmap emulation (1.5-2.4x gap) understates the stock-mmap gap; true stock llama.cpp mmap not measured by us

title: The Other Half of the Memory Wall: Serving 35B MoEs from SSD with Trained Routing Prediction (Edge0; Lin, Wang, Cai, Liu, Zeng; AutoArk)
setup: Qwen3.6-35B-A3B 40 layers x 256 experts, base K=8 released at K=4, int4 g64, 19.5 GB; also Ling 3.0 tiny 24x128 K=8; Mac mini M4 Pro 24GB (Table 1), MacBook M2 16GB (prerouter A/B), MLX only, SSD bandwidth not stated, batch 1; trained per-layer prerouter + unmerged LoRA r=16

catalog_numbers_correct.true_value: 3.9 is the fully resident server; the paper's on-demand arm on that machine is 19.9 tok/s
abstract says so, but own data: 19.9 tok/s on 24GB; on 16GB M2 on-demand is 3.5 tok/s vs 6.4
avg of 5 benchmarks, includes int4 + K=4 + routing replacement

catalog_numbers_correct.claim: first pass body note: 3.9 is resident

why: Apple MLX, trained prerouter and LoRA per model, K halved (lossy), 24GB machine where resident model nearly fills RAM; prefetch gain ~3% where memory is not tight; our 125B top-10 has no retraining path.
quality_loss: avg -4.0 points (79.2 vs 83.2) over AIME/HumanEval/GPQA-D/MMLU-Pro/IFBench; AIME -6.1 (35B), -10.0 (8B)
ablation: yes: prerouter vs on-demand at K=2/4/8, prerouter on/off, incremental stacking +34%, LoRA merged vs unmerged; no cache vs layout split
limitations: single FIFO request, batching unmodelled, decode CPU-bound (44 ms graph build floor), gains shrink on hot caches/fast storage, adjacent-token agreement ~1/4, prerouter takes unreclaimable residency, MLX only
contradicts_our_findings: Do not use 3.9 as evidence that naive streaming fails; paper's own on-demand streaming is 19.9 tok/s on 24GB
